marquee: *** Kia Ora! *** Welcome to our New Zealand travel log! *** -- Keeks & Elsie

posts.title: Friday, 4/3 - Sunday 4/5: Blenheim Surf ‘n’ Paint, Ferry, Wellington Easter
posts.body:
Woke up in Blenheim on Friday and decided to check the beach nearby before heading back to Kaikoura to definitively score waves (which we did, see two posts ago). As we crested the hill towards the beach (and fishtailed down the unmarked dirt road), it was clear that the winds were offshore and something was surfable.


Slow but deliberate breakfast crafted of the usual: fried eggs, sausage varietals, and cheese on toasted croissants (had these every day).



Enjoyed a post-breakfast shirtless board-shorts session on Elsie’s longboard. Nothing to write home about, but hard to resist a self-discovered backlit waist-high wave.


Took turns surfing and being photographer/content creator. Then, as wetsuits dried, painted the scene:


**********************************************


Back in Blenheim on Saturday after a quick Friday night Kaikoura excursion. We ventured to Fromm Winery for a full vineyard tour and wine tasting I set up for us to get the authentic Marlborough experience. Fromm is unique in Marlborough as the only vineyard to specialize in something other than Sauvignon Blanc, and is very small.



We were led around enthusiastically by Stephen, who at the age of 60 changed careers to vineyard work. He mentioned he hand picked something like 6 tons of grapes last year alone. Keeks and I both had a lot of fun nerding out with Stephen, learning about everything from grafting root stalks to protect against phylloxera to the fact that you might die from lack of oxygen if you fell asleep in the “burping room.”



Keeks the Gentleman chauffeured us from cellardoor to ferryboat. Joining the herd to line up for the boat contrasted with hermit van life of the last two weeks. But it was fun to cross a gnarly strait of water and continue our adventure without knowing where we’d sleep that night (and any night thereafter, or before!).



Sunset dinner as we left the fjorded South Island: leftover smoked salmon from Good Friday (best enjoyed out of the van in public), croissants, green olives, cafe French fries and lots of cheese. Parked on the side of the road after cruising through downtown Wellington.




The next day began with Easter Mass at St. Mary’s of the Angels. We were seated right behind the choir, who weren’t dressed differently from us normies—funny to see them immediately start ripping hymns on beat 1. Had a nice conversation with the priest outside afterwards.

Then went to meet Elsie’s Burning Man Kiwi friends, Georgia and Richard, and new friend Hugo (their 15-month-old son)! We caught up over hot cross buns, feijoa fruit, and lattes on their patio. Then had playtime on the playground across the street. Tossed feijoas around with Hugo and Elsie snapped a film pic of the three of them!

Off to Taranaki we go!

posts.title: Thursday, 4/2: Elsie’s Blenheim Buzzer Beater
posts.body:
Kicked it up from Kaikoura to Blenheim after thinking we were getting too comfortable in Kaikoura. Quickly realized this wasn’t the vibe after driving through a maze of RV and tractor dealerships. However, Blenheim is smack-dab in the middle of Marlborough, New Zealand’s most famous wine region, and is near some fishy waters, including the first gin clear spring creek we have seen.


Legend has it this spring-fed stream holds massive trout (legend also confirmed by a deep-think AI query). However, when we probed it through polarized lenses at several access points, we ended up fishless and wet from tussock trodding. What a beautiful experience, though—despite being heavily vegetated, the stream lacked any algae or sediment whatsoever. It was crystal clear, 10 feet wide on average, incredibly deep, and nearly silent as it meandered through grass banks.


After exhausting the spring creek option, the sun was getting low and we felt our chances of seeing fish without sandfly assault were diminishing. So we made a dinner reservation at a nearby vineyard to protect against the creep of dusk. Left us just enough time to drive the van onto a large freestone riverbank to try one more spot…


Walked past a local gentleman, born and raised in Blenheim, taking his dog (named Gerald or something similar) for a sunset swim. He directed us to a few pockets of water near his dog’s swim and provided some fly recommendations. His enthusiasm for almost all the flies in our box conveyed that he was either very “dialed” or didn’t know what he was doing. “Dialed” or “fishy” people love to say things to the effect of, “yeah, that’ll catch fish”, since they’ve caught fish in every scenario with every fly in their pouch at that spot.

We wandered upstream across grapefruit-sized freestones to a shallow pool and waded barefoot to the edge of the bankside eddy. The cool water relieved our ankles and calves which were covered in sandfly bites. After a few cautious dryfly drifts, some time to let our eyes adjust, and some missed takes, it was time for a fly change. The dinner bell was creeping in. Keeks rushed to swap flies and in doing so, dropped the mayfly imitation (fly to be switched to) into the flowing water beneath us. “Watch this be the right fly,” Keeks said. We both watched the new fly lazily float directly downstream towards the spot a fish had previously risen and—slurp! We started dying laughing. “Now we know what fly to use.”

Elsie casted and re-casted persistently, drifting the new fly through each lane of the riffle. Small fish rose more fervently—some even cleared the water—but seemed to prefer real mayflies over her imitation. A few “we should really go”s and “one more cast”-s later, I turned away and began to slowly wade back toward the rocky riverbank, hoping Elsie would conjure some buzzer beater dinner bell fish magic.


I turned around to find Elsie’s face stolen and her rod bent! “I think I’m on?!” A small silver flash lept at the end of the leader. I speed-waded over as she stripped the fish in. It swam a few loops around us, almost tangling. I netted it. A perfect little rainbow with a Spinner fly in the corner of its mouth.


Elsie spent a moment with it, posing for a quick pic and release vid. The low sun illuminated the greens and purples in a totally unique way.


And Elsie’s shiny hand jewelry.


It was a happy, smiley, victorious walk back to the car and evening thereafter.

posts.title: Friday, 3/27 - Saturday, 4/4. “O, Kaikoura!”
posts.body:
Mountains spire o’er rugged reefs
And harbored boats float unbroken swell.
Cozy pubs serve mussels and beefs
For passersthrough and seamen that dwell

Throughout the year or just the eve,
Kaikoura’s comfort was ne’er earned.
It took seven days to leave,
And in my mind its surf-side fires still burn.



********************************************************************


**The above pic is film! Can you believe it?**

The best time was sharing an empty left reef point break all to ourselves after “discovering” it. Elsie pioneered this spot a few days earlier with a questionably possible water entry through a reef rock and bull kelp minefield. She gracefully paddled out for a two-wave session without hiccups while I took pics from the rocks. Knee to waist high lined up lefts for 75yds.


Days later, with more swell and more favorable wind, we found ourselves frantically fleeing the van to paddle out. Mid day sun, everyone else surfing the right about a mile away. Head high to overhead, more or less glassy 100yd rides. Crumbled over the main rock for a gentle takeoff, sometimes extended boogie takeoff, ample time to set up. Then predictable walled and flatter sections all the way down. Fish with large keels worked for huge cutbacks. Funky backwash section on the inside as the tide came in if you didn’t take the first wave of the set. Dreadhead kook paddled out and complimented our surfing. Surfed for two hours and then tide and swell abruptly shut down.


In order to get acquainted with this town, we first had to explore the yarn store, then eat nasty fried fish while seagulls stalked our unattended fries. After initiation, we settled in to a no-frills beachside lot just feet away from two of Kaikoura’s main breaks.




The days really blended together. AM beachfront wakeups, countless surfs, coffee and hot breakfast, followed by an interlude of dishes and debating whether to go into town to try on that pink possum sweater. Always followed up with a drive over to the crowded—yet beautifully consistent—right point break backdropped with snowcapped mountains to surf again. Then, back to the lot to do the reverse into and after sunset.


Ended up leaving town for Blenheim after convincing ourselves we had stayed too long. The trip was fruitful because Elsie caught a fish! and we indulged in a delicious meal at a winery (separate entry). But…… the mysterious mountainwave magnetism of Kaikoura called, and within 24 hours of departing, we were back, surfing our most memorable sessions at The Left and Mangamaunu (morning longboard baby wave sesh).

Other moments include:



* Beach fires in front of the main break

* Lots and lots of film photos—stay tuned! **update** we've posted throughout!

* Epic shelling session in the rain; wet shells easier to see on account of sparkles
* Trying out some pretty mediocre restaurants

* A day of chores

* Finding pretty silver jewelry for Elsie with seashells

* Solid van meals
* Nighttime slow shutter light painting—stay tuned!
* Buying matching NZ made pocket knives at Hunting & Fishing store
* Continually pondering if we would go back and try on that pink possum sweater

posts.title: Thursday 3/26 - Friday 3/27. Jake and Kathy’s place
posts.body:
It’s helpful to know how many limbs someone has that are claws before meeting them in a public beachside parking lot.

We had arranged to meet up with good friends of good friends, who live off-grid in a yurt on a hemp farm north of Westport.



Elsie and I watched the waves from bed while waiting on further meetup comms from Jake. Then went a “tick-tick” on the window from a claw at the end of a large bearded man’s arm—Elsie gasped and then asked, “do you know him?”

It had to be Jake, so we opened the sliding door and were quick to shoot the breeze. Jake was eye-level with us despite the van’s two-foot height advantage. He gave us the lay of the land, and the punchline was “don’t tell anyone about this place”.

The tight-knit nature of Jake and Kathy’s community shined through his quippy remarks and his infectious cackle. Within 30 minutes, it was clear Jake and Kathy (who we hadn’t even met yet!) have given love and labor to their community over decades to be able to generously offer hospitality and fun activities to near strangers.

Their setup is so unique, living fully *among* the raw west coast rainforest. Before we knew it, we were enclosed by rain on all sides but sheltered by the yurt’s covered patio. And there, we held court for hours, drinking beers and eating grapes from Kathy’s friend’s farm.



A restful night in the van tucked into a cleared portion of their land allowed for an even more enjoyable morning. We joined Jake and Kathy in their home for breakfast and “f*ckawfee” and even more stories. These two should really write a book.


Jake and Kathy sent us off with a bag of grapes and tomatoes, well-exercised laughing muscles, and a groovy new band to check out. Finally, Jake made sure to let us know that if we ever got lost, all we had to do was navigate to the West Coast, turn right, and ask for the no-legged man with a beer in his claw-arm.

P.S. snapped a film portrait of Jake and Kathy, will post when developed
--> Update: this has been uploaded as the cover photo!

posts.title: Wednesday 3/25 - van stuck next to pumping surf, lunch surf, Hwy 1-type surf discovery
posts.body:
Woke up next to low tide offshore clean but not super walled beach break. Wind and swell was supposed to cooperate as the day progressed, so enjoyed coffee and hot brekky on the beach. FaceTimed Bea and her new kitten!! She seems eager to meet Biggie and the crew. Packed up shop and headed north along the coastal highway north of Greymouth.

Another rainless, fair weather day under the persistent high above NZ.

The road was a fair bit more coastal with frequent views of coves, rock fingers, and empty waves. Still rugged, mountainous, and weaves through verdant rainforest.


We pulled off after watching a rocky point produce a few nice lefts that connected to the beach break. We rolled the van down a narrow, steep dirt road labeled “beach” by piece of painted driftwood. The road ended abruptly into loose, palm-sized shingle stones. With no way back to the road other than reverse, we attempted a turnaround and immediately got both sets of wheels stuck. The stuck position was quite pathetic but very stuck.




Used sticks to dig out and then jammed them in behind for traction. Waves were reeling by. After 45 minutes of sandfly attack while digging, Elsie successfully reversed the van out of its hole while I pushed.


We reversed van up the steep beach road, parked up the street, and enjoyed a nice surf. Glassy. Elsie achieved rhythm with some waves to the inside. I felt great on board with these larger fins. Fall more when leash is attached.


We trucked north, through rainforest, mountains, and coastline, heads on swivels at every visible section of the water below. Stopped after Elsie spotted a sea run brown trout in crystal clear water near the river mouth. Can’t just drive past so we took a few casts and spotted more fish. They did not take much interest in the menu of flies presented.


We speed-ran the tour walk at Pancake Rocks—which is supposed to last 20 minutes—in under 10. Jerry Garcia/Hagrid/Jeff Mattson sighting.

Continued north beyond Punakaiki. Fog banks softened the horizon line and distant breaking waves, remaining unmoved due to lack of wind. Several pull-offs and “could be fun”s later, we decided to get in the water at a mellow bay near Westport. Rocks guarded its mouth, acting as a filter for unwanted swell directions. On the left, the result was a clean, Cardiff-like outer bar that broke gently on takeoff, turned into a rippable wall for two-ish turns, ending in a beachside close out section. The right did the same thing without the end section, and broke around a rock halfway through the ride.


A few folks in the lineup. We’ve only surfed at two “crowded” spots—five to fifteen people—and both of them included a 45-year-old with a buzz cut riding a yellowing short board exceeding 6’3 in length. Elsie paddle-battled some older local regulators for the outside bombs. Fun party-waving the inside reform section within the rocks to close out the sesh.

Buzzer-beatered grocery store closing to grab ingredients for a well deserved muck of lamb sausage, Greek/feta salad, and the rare find of Kraft Mac & cheese. Slept at a packed freedom camping spot on the beach.

posts.title: Tuesday 3/24 - Kea birds, west coast, impeccable sunset session
posts.body:
Woke in the dark on high alert due to yesterday’s sandfly panic and kea birds swarming van at the sound of my alarm. Each creature has notoriety on the west coast for being pesky. Sandfly is a barely visible biter, and Kea bird will gnaw at car parts if it senses food.



Rushed out of there, heading north through misty inland dawn over rough, barely grazed pastureland and tumbled down shack homes. Low fuel levels snuck up on us due to repeated mountain climbs and descents. Paid lots of money for bacon, egg, no cheese on white toast, and coffees where we could fuel. Worth not having to stop and cook.





Wove in, out, up, and down and finally reached a spot south of Greymouth exuding sun-kissed glory and a comfortable higher humidity than we have experienced.


Nice to air out the van and paddle out to an empty beach break. Unfortunately strong southerly current made for an unpleasant paddle upstream.

Headed north and pulled up to a spot that wedged with lots of Hector’s dolphins playing in the waves. Nice to walk, talk, and feel the wind.

Around the corner was a decadent little break that looked a lot like a popular reefy longboard spot on Long Island. Tide was high and it was clear this had potential with a lower tide. Variety of waves and corners to takeoff on. But the featured one was notably the left which, similar to the Long Island spot when good, walls all the way from peak to beach, and uniquely continues breaking past spectator point on the beach.


After tanning and applying a healthy dose of Sun-In, we leisurely paddled out. Despite her illness, Elsie connected on several waves, and importantly connected with her board. Turns, noserides, speedy high lines.



I snapped some pics from the beach after caching a fast, flowy one and feeling rock-solid on the new fish, which was now featuring larger keels. In this session I found that going leashless is the key to unlocking a new board; give yourself no other option but to pause, take stock, and make no movements other than those your board permits you to.


Dreamy rest of the evening as the sun set bright orange in the northwest. Chatted with Tim, who was taking pics on the beach. He lives in Canterbury.

posts.title: Monday 3/23 - Queenstown high life, sandfly panic attacks on river, headed west
posts.body:
Our morning in Queenstown consisted of a search for coffee and finding an excuse not to go paragliding. Many tourist shops that all sell the exact same thing later, we headed to the gondola with matching possum merino hats and three alpaca fur kiwi birds in hand. Panoramic views of the city and massive glacial lake made the trip up well worth it.



By the time we got to the top, I still hadn’t found a reason not to paraglide, so off I went with Dom, a 50 year old lifelong flyer. Running off the side of a cliff was the scariest part, but once you’re gliding through the air, it was quite relaxing.


Dom then handed me the parachute handles and instructed me on how to do spins and it got much more exhilarating from there. Loops and spins took us horizontal to the city looking straight down fearing the wind won’t pull us back up. 10 minutes later, we touched down in a big grassy field.


Queenstown can’t get any more exciting than that, so we dismounted by washing the van and setting out for the rugged, mysterious, sandfly-infested West Coast. Wasn’t too long until we were rubbernecking at the sight of crystal clear water. Elsie spotted a fish from the road, so we began navigating the best point of entry to this river.

After shimmying down a steep, grassy, trailless hillside, we speedwalked to the nearest sunlit pool (farther than it initially appeared, and decreased in area due to the receding sun). Before we knew it, sandflies enveloped each of our personal spaces and Keeks was sweating while trying to undo a panic induced knot.




We exchanged one look and began speedwalking even faster back to the van, which was much farther away than it seemed, swatting sandflies along the way. We ended up whacking through thorns, wading through tiny tributaries, Elsie’s sickness had not improved, and Keeks took a rusty nail to his thigh (by a miracle, the nail did not penetrate pant fabric, despite penetrating skin fairly deeply).

Made it back to the car defeated and covered in fresh bug bites. Initial plan was to stay here, but given the crises faced, we decided to push to the west coast, as far away from this nightmare as possible.


Gorgeous rest of the drive over mountain passes with glacial and gorge visions. Made it through Haast by dark and decided to sleep at next available campsite, one more hour north.

posts.title: Sunday 3/22 - Five Rivers Road - Queenstown pilgrimage. Pull-off fishing success. Finally showered.
posts.body:
Waves were kind of reeling at 3am. Resembled a certain east coast right point within hours of NYC. Back to bed. The surf itch remained unscratched at dawn when the wind and tide repeated themselves from the prior evening. So we decided to trade the vagabond surf chase for the first world amenities of Queenstown.



Not long after our departure from the southernmost point of the South Island, we stopped the car on account of fishy waters. We had just turned onto Five Rivers Road, and this was either River #1 or River #5. Half of our group expressed reluctance to get on the water due to flu-like symptoms. Nevertheless, the sun was up, the wind was calm, and “we’re in New Zealand”. Within five minutes, the other half of the group had landed a small brown trout on a dry fly. Unfortunately for the flu-having half, this meant we were to stay on the river until either a very large brown trout was landed or the fishermen suffered defeat…



Haphazardly hooked a very large fish while leaving fly in the water stepping downstream. Landed the fish but missed pic of it in-hand. Elsie went on a valiant goose chase along—and in—the river for a film pic but fish had slipped out by the time we connected. Snapped one picture mid-fight. Zoom in for size and detail.


Back on the road, we stopped at a junction cafe/petting zoo. Elsie finally got to pet a sheep, thus confirming they are in fact NOT AI. Caffeinated and vibes replenished.



The sight of an historic coal fired passenger train approaching its station was our next distraction, taking us off the road. Fate would have it that the train station was a few hundred yards away from more incredibly fishy water at River #3-ish.



The river was gin clear and very slow moving with 2ft-deep pools max. Within a quarter mile of our walk along the stream, we spotted a nicely sized fish, grazing the pool for bugs both above and suspended in the water column. His claimed pool was no deeper than 18 inches.


We crawled up to about 25 feet from the river’s edge. My first cast was short and thankfully the fish had turned away right before it landed. He looped the perimeter of the pool again and we waited for the next approach. Very similar to fishing saltwater flats. Second cast landed five feet in front of the fish. Seeing it, the fish redirected course towards us, opened and then closed his mouth. He had taken the nymph. Before the dryfly even went under, I set the hook and a short fight commenced. Not many obstacles. Landed without a net in shallower water. It all happened like an Orvis book or Jensen Fly Fishing video. Also fun to be wet wading in Merrells and jeans. Side profile of fish held in traditional stance is on film camera so stay tuned for that. ** Update, see cover photo! **




Afterwards, even despite illness, we were fired up and eager to catch another. We battled wind and lower sun angle (first fish landed around 5pm), with a few opportunities for a hook-up on sighted fish but nothing connected. Elsie had one picture perfect cast between bankside willow trees that was refused.


We ended the day at a legitamite holiday park in Queenstown. Washed the van. Laundry felt good. Showers felt great. Delish Italian restaurant on the water. Trout and eels visible in the lake below. Gelato and cold medicine night cap. Elsie rescued a hedgehog from the middle of the street!

posts.title: Saturday 3/21 - Chill AM, Headed West
posts.body:
Slow morning as the sun crept over the beach. We woke with the sun, but too cozy to move Keeks watched the waves as I dozed in and out of sleep. I felt kind of sick this morning so it took me a while to get motivated. After minutes of watching what appeared to be knee high waves roll in, we noticed that the waves were much bigger, and barreling? We saw a silhouette race across a hollow left towards the far left side of the beach and decided to paddle out.


This session brought some challenges. The bigger waves were the ones that were working but they were steep and fast, pretty intimidating for me. I caught a couple but they spit me out the back because I wasn’t feeling confident charging down the face. I had more of a paddle session turned atomic washing machine at the end as I took a huge set to the head trying to get out of the water. 2 hours later I still have water pouring out of my nose and sand coming out of me ears. Yet, it’s always an opportunity to learn!

Keeks had difficulty too, but managed to find a couple quick lefts. One potential close-to-barreled moment on a just-overhead set wave. Experimented up the point close to the rocks. Experiment yielded no significant results.

Breakfast was firing. Egg scramble with peppers, salami, and parm. We finally nailed the coffee, which required pressure and scalding hot water. We’ve been mixing in NZ whole milk to our coffee. Wholy Moly it’s delicious and creamy. Two women in a horse-drawn buggy cruiser through the campsite and down a rocky dirt road to the beach. They crossed the small river crossing and the horse began to lope across the flat sand. Buggy exceeded what we thought was max speed for that vehicle. Then they disappeared.

Cleaned dishes, packed up our half wet gear hanging from various perches on our van, and mentally prepared to check Long Point to redeem a session that didn’t meet flow state expectations. My hopes were high, given the wind was supposed to switch offshore and swell was forecast to stay exactly the same. And we’d be arriving at the right tide. We got stuck behind the horse and buggy on our way out. They were blessed with the bliss of having no rear view mirror, and continued on, cruising the middle of the road through gorgeous pastures. No rear view mirror is probably a nice way to live life.

We rounded the corner and the down-the-point vista was an underwhelming scene. Shorter period, smaller, and crumbly due to light onshore wind. Waves were barely breaking off the big rock they were breaking off the day before—at high tide. Not the offshore glory we rolled up on yesterday. We gave it about an hour on a pulloff at the top of the hill, buying time with the distracting simple pleasure of cell service. Using our phones felt like leaving the office for a smoke break—a complete offspeed pitch. We posted the first few days’ blogs. We checked the swell, wind, and tide. The farmer let his sheep out into a new field, which required moving them along the road on which we were parked. As they encircled the van, they bahhed loudly. A group of people on horseback rode by.

After reaching a good screen time stopping point we walked out to check for improvements in the surf. The wind had improved slightly, but the swell had dropped almost entirely. Not worth paddling out for at all. Heartbreak set in. Really wanted a film picture of this gorgeous break. Even more so, really wanted to score it. I thought if you put in the time and are willing to drive, you are bound to score! Lesson learned is similar that of the surfboard fin sampling menu: there’s a good chance what you’re surfing now is the best it will get.

We quickly pivoted, finding purpose in “let’s just go (south)west”. Moderate swell from the SW and winds from the SW/W meant that right points and properly sheltered breaks would be working over there. We were also encouraged by Surfline’s 4-5ft rated green for the next several days at many of these southwestern spots. With lots to look forward to, we left Long Point in the rearview mirror.

Drive was a struggle on several hours of dirt road, as we discovered a leak somewhere in the van was letting in dust kicked up by our get-west haste. NASCAR pit stopped at a grocery store (10 minute restock) and carried on to check spots matching the east facing description.

Flat again! This heartbreak, though, unlike the one at Long Point amplified by caffeine, was buffered by drive fatigue and prior heartbreak. Elsie filed a report of the Report on Surfline, which claimed that contrary to the 4-5ft Surfline contented, the swell was 0ft. We drove on. Pulled into a farmer’s driveway to request access to check waves. Gorgeous setup. Ungorgeous waves.


Great shelling session at sunset into dark. Elsie found several paua (abalone) specimen and a perfectly round frisbee shaped rock. Chat gpt says it’s greywhack. Paua will be coming home with us to be tumbled.

posts.title: Friday 3/20 - Deep Catlins River walk, trout, Long Point surf
posts.body:
Woke in the forest at a wet muddy campground, downstream from where we bushwhacked up yesterday. Packed PBBJs, some fruit, and headed upstream. The far bank was sheep grazing land. Close bank, where the trail was, was a gnarly rooted craggy cliffside goat path. The sign says “River walk”. We “walked” five and half miles up, down, sideways, in the river, out of the river.

Again, God was present. There is maybe no other way to describe it. Your skin feels cradled by the air. Moss-covered logs and stones look like perfect napping places. And you’d probably be fine doing so. Everything looks perfectly placed in calming chaos, colors and shapes complementing each other in a serene composition. The palm-looking ferns of five feet in height made for a friendly obstacle to walk around and over between trail and river. Whereas in New England you’d be covered in ticks after these maneuvers, here, you feel cleaner than before you left the car.


I caught another, slightly larger brown on a perfect drift directly upstream of me. We’re trudged on seeking new water. No further fish. Walk back was tough and limbs and joints were hurting. We made it back to the van very happy, with no serious injuries.

“Are-we-missing-waves?”-anxiety set in and we made a quick transition to Long Point, half expecting it to be flat. The van rounded the corner after crossing into private land and the view up the point emerged. Overhead, offshore, sectiony but makeable lefts rolling down the point. Cobalt Blue sunlit water. One guy out. Saw him get an insane one for at least 75 yards.


We hiked across a wind-whipped hillside covered in spiky prickly feet pokers, overheating in our fully zipped suits with boards in hand. Must have been 30min. Ran into the guy and his friend on their way back. “High tide soon, you might get lucky up the point though. It was barreling earlier.”

Empowered to race against the tide, I walked through a patch of six-foot-tall sawgrass and sliced my toe. It bled fairly rapidly for about three minutes until we reached the spot and then wrapped a cotton fabric tourniquet for compression. Then Sunk Cost fallacy set in: we hiked all that way, and there are waves right there. I’m going surfing.




It was a bit too heavy and the wave broke close to the jagged rocks on shore for the longboard, so Elsie hung on the beach wearing a Survivor-styled Buff and the bottom half of her wetsuit while I paddled out through a keyhole in the reef. Kelp on either side of me, dragging across the surface in and out with each wave. Big, thick, dark kelp.

The takeoff spot at high tide was all the way up the point. On a boil above a rock surrounded by kelp. One piece of kelp sticking out that, when a wave came and flipped its orientation, flopped a little kelp tail up in the air behind it, and then disappeared below the surface. Like a seal because it had a split tail. Kelp seal.

Waves roped along like kelp, down the point, groomed by the now quite heavy offshore E wind. I had a few overhead waves and some out of control turns.


I don’t feel confident in the board quite yet. Lazy Lightning was skittish and twitchy with the EN fins. I was out of balance and out of whack with hands flailing in a bad looking way. Fortunately, I was unaware of this until after I came in. Completely buzzed and psyched about a dream session, I reviewed videos that Elsie captured. Nothing to ruin a perfect session more than videos of yourself (which of course, you always want). The day I refuse to have my surfing the subject of any digital content will be celebrated by all. It’s really not self deprecating for attention—I know that I had fun gliding across the waves. And I know that I’m probably not capable of much more than my performance out there. It’s just that I thought I looked way cooler doing it.

Capped off another stellar day, this one a bit more full of challenges and physical endurance, at PK bay again. Grilled burgers, peppers, onions, zucchini. Carrots and hummus on the side. Snapped a nicely composed film pic of Elsie and she grabbed one of the cliffside. Elsie chatted with the girls in her photo holding surfboards. One from Christchurch, other from Colorado. Both in college in Dunedin. Friends! We’ll send them the pic when developed. ** Update, see below!! **





A few campfires, high school aged group playing and singing songs with guitar. A decent number of campers here on Friday night. Goodnight!

posts.title: Thursday 3/19 - pre-breakfast surf at PK Bay, NZ trout on day 4. Catlins Day 2.
posts.body:
Sheep surrounding the van when we woke up. Hector’s Dolphins surrounding us while surfing. Offshore, waist/chest high, backlit steep hollow beach break with a massive cliff face enclosing the open ocean around us. Not lining up perfectly but incredible scenery and friendly local (dolphin) vibes. Had one notable wave on new fish with a trim across a flat section and a redirecting roundhouse toward the curl.





After breakfast, I miscalculated the wind and we checked Long Point. The wind still had some S in it. Drove south to check some more spots and came up short surf-wise, but struck gold in a gadget and gizmo shop that served coffee and had a house guitar.


Elsie got some sea glass earrings, a “birds of New Zealand” book, and a latte while I strummed. We checked out a nearby waterfall.





Made it a plan to come back to long point tomorrow when the wind switched, and in the meantime, try to fish. Drove up the catlins river, through rolling farmland (per usual — it’s everywhere), breaking branches and stepping on limbs to get the van through an unmarked road that, on the map, appeared to be closer to good water. There are few pockets of good cell service, so we navigated based on a half loaded Google Map and some decent intuition, because we ended up finding a trail that wound down a steep canyon to the river.

It was plunge pool riffle run heaven. Light dancing, moss glowing, biodiversity thriving. We kept remarking that it felt like game of thrones, lord of the rings, ACOTAR books, Hunger Games, because of the magical God-is-with-me feeling of walking through this backcountry. Underpinning this sensation was the peculiar realization that this was a comfortable, safe place. No predators, insects were not a problem, and the temperature(s) was perfect. “The air was 70 degrees, the water was 70 degrees…” except the water was slightly cooler and more refreshing and conducive to trout cohabitation (Endless Summer). It smelled of waterfall and unsweetened honeysuckle, if that existed—and if it did exist, it would probably be here.





Crosshairs were focused on sight fishing, so we moved slowly upstream with no casts. At our lunch/turning around spot, we threw some casts. I hooked up on one of the first casts using a Parachute Adams. There were a few mayflies buzzing around. Landed a small brown trout that had silvery big-spotted sea-run features. They are known to run out to the Catlins Lake, an estuary, and back up the river. A rad DIY self-guide and bushwhack potential sea run, but definitely brown, trout.


Then started casting at all fishy water on the way back. On the next pool, I got broken off by a 3-5lb brown that rose on the PA 30ft out. Since the little brown I landed earlier was slightly underwhelming (wanted to sight it and wanted it to be big fat and golden brown), this fish was definitely proper enough to warrant another chase tomorrow.

Bushwhacked back and down the road to a campsite lower on the river and cooked butter chicken. Delicious. Didn’t make it to dessert before zonking.

posts.title: Wednesday 3/18 - Dunedin area and Catlins Day 1
posts.body:
Checked north of Dunedin in Warrington given SW wind. Super small so did not get in, but great open-door van vibes with a playground nearby, warm sun, breeze, lushness in a small neighborhood. Lots of seashells to play with too. Plen air’d the scene.


We were itching to surf so decided to high tail it south to the rugged Catlins. Stocked up at grocery store, last minute items in surf shop, gas, Starbucks. We wandered into a photo store and chatted with the owner until he brought out a fully manual Canon film camera from the back. Asking price was about half of what these go for in the US, so we purchased it along with two rolls of film. Owner threw in a polarizing filter too. Then we headed South.

The drive was incredible. Golden hour seemed to last 3 hours.



Checked cannibal bay, wind was too S.

Arrived at the most beautiful campsite at PK Bay and jumped in the water for a swim. Watched the shadows rise on the headlands as the sun set, cooked pasta bolognese, and crashed. Another full night’s sleep.

posts.title: Tuesday 3/17 - Mellow score on the way to Dunedin, south of a lighthouse. Long exploratory afternoon in Dunedin
posts.body:
As the sun came up, what resembled the rolling green hills of Upstate NY (the area around Christchurch) transformed into temperate tropical Mediterranean coastal bucolic magic. The van charged on through dawn, through vast expanses of sheep meadows and weird cypress trees. We pulled up on a gorgeous, glass, back-lit waist high beach break with nobody in sight—and decided to break the number one rule (“don’t leave fish to find fish”) by leaving this 7am beach break splendor to check out a lighthouse that may have had a point break.

The detour was an excellent sight-seeing decision but a poor surf guiding one. The lighthouse was painted white and barely cleared the variety of palms and other strange fake-looking real trees. Appeared to be, like many lighthouses, not technologically relevant due to its small stature and positioning set far back on the hill. Makes it a much more interesting lighthouse. Fur seals lined the bay and barked and laughed in the sun. Elsie enjoyed their company but I felt they were rubbing it in. We stopped for a quick photo shoot at the top of the hill and the headed back to the beach break.


We paddled out and had ourselves a mellow score of a session, which was the debut of Elsie’s custom and my handshape. Everybody happy. Board will take some getting used to, but has the potential for greatness. Squirts with speed in small stuff and flat sections but TBD in bigger stuff. Sampled a few fins and will likely end up where I started (K2 or some small keel). Elsie’s board is light, maneuverable, and importantly has what seems to be the right curves and concanves in the right places. Cool airplane takeoff feeling from the nose concave.


After making breakfast and coffee in front of the spot, we drove south, arriving in Dunedin in the afternoon. We landed at a break in town that was howling offshore. Checked a few spots on the peninsula that were way too windy but the act of checking was enjoyable — perched on a high headland, walked through a field of sheep.




Then checked Black Head, a spot south of Dunedin. Some barrel opportunities but few and far between and very windy. Did not paddle out.

St Paddy’s dinner in Dunedin at Italian spot in front of town surf spot St Clair. Chatted with bartender who was an American doing a postgrad in geology at U Otago. He had only been in NZ for a year, and had already adopted lots of the lingo. Also kind of sounded like he was forcing an accent which made us giggle.


Drove to Smaills beach lot to sleep — a spot on the peninsula — but was gusting so hard that the van tipping over was a genuine concern. We were so tired and delirious that when Elsie raised this issue, I said “yeah but at least we’ll tip sideways and not off the cliff”. We moved to a parking lot in front of St Clair, the break in town, shortly after. Full night’s sleep.

posts.title: Monday 3/16 - Arrived!
posts.body:
Long travel day included an 18 hour flight from JFK > AKL, one failed approach into Christchurch due to fog, doubled back to Auckland, and one successful landing. Met a surfer flying through to Brisbane who was an engineer on Qantas now spending his pension flight miles.

Picked up the van, loaded up on groceries, and picked up Elsie’s board, which she had custom made by a local dude. Drove through and out of Christchurch, which was aglow with a blanket of warm Indian Summer. Leaves had started to change but it was 70 and sunny. Slept at beach parking lot a few hours south of Christchurch.
